--- title: "Building and sharing a SummarizedExperiment" author: - name: Sean Davis url: https://seandavi.github.io/ affiliation: University of Colorado
Anschutz School of Medicine affiliation-url: https://medschool.cuanschutz.edu/ email: seandavi@gmail.com --- In the [previous chapter](bioc-summarizedexperiment.qmd) you worked with a `SummarizedExperiment` someone else had assembled — the `airway` dataset, ready to subset and plot. But a great deal of real data does *not* arrive that way. It arrives as a spreadsheet: a few columns describing the genes, a wall of numeric columns holding the measurements, and the sample information living only in your head or a separate file. Turning that loose table into a proper `SummarizedExperiment` is one of the most useful things you can do, because from that point on the object keeps itself consistent — and it speaks the same language as every Bioconductor analysis package you'll reach for next. In this chapter you'll build a `SummarizedExperiment` from raw parts, add a derived assay, draw a clustered heatmap, and then save and share the result so a collaborator gets everything in a single file. ## What you'll learn By the end of this chapter you will be able to: - Assemble a `SummarizedExperiment` from a matrix (or several), a feature table, and a sample table — and explain the alignment rules the constructor enforces. - Add a **derived assay** (e.g. a normalized or log-ratio matrix) that stays aligned to the originals. - Select informative (variable) features and draw an unsupervised clustering heatmap. - **Save** an experiment to one file and **share** it, provenance and all, with `saveRDS()`/`readRDS()`. - Explain why this one object plugs into the wider Bioconductor ecosystem. ::: {.callout-tip} ## Installing the packages ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} BiocManager::install(c("SummarizedExperiment", "pheatmap")) ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: ## The ingredients To construct a `SummarizedExperiment` you supply: - `assays`: one or more matrices (or matrix-like objects) of data — the numbers; - `rowData`: a `DataFrame` describing the features (rows); - `colData`: a `DataFrame` describing the samples (columns); - optionally `metadata`: a list of anything else about the experiment. We'll build one from the **DeRisi** dataset — a classic yeast microarray time course measuring gene expression as cells exhaust their glucose and switch metabolic gears (the *diauxic shift*). It begins life as a plain `data.frame`: the first two columns identify each gene, and the rest are measurements. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(SummarizedExperiment) deRisi <- read.csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/seandavi/RBiocBook/main/data/derisi.csv") head(deRisi) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ORF Name R1 R2 R3 R4 R5 R6 R7 R1.Bkg R2.Bkg R3.Bkg 1 YHR007C ERG11 7896 7484 14679 14617 9853 7599 6490 1155 1984 1323 2 YBR218C PYC2 12144 11177 10241 4820 4950 7047 17035 1074 1694 1243 3 YAL051W FUN43 4478 6435 6230 6848 5111 7180 4497 1140 1950 1649 4 YAL053W 6343 8243 6743 3304 3556 4694 3849 1020 1897 1196 5 YAL054C ACS1 1542 3044 2076 1695 1753 4806 10802 1082 1940 1504 6 YAL055W 1769 3243 2094 1367 1853 3580 1956 975 1821 1185 R4.Bkg R5.Bkg R6.Bkg R7.Bkg G1 G2 G3 G4 G5 G6 G7 G1.Bkg 1 1171 914 2445 981 8432 7173 11736 16798 12315 16111 13931 2404 2 876 1211 2444 742 11509 10226 13372 6500 6255 9024 6904 2148 3 1183 898 2637 927 5865 5895 5345 6302 5400 7933 5026 2422 4 881 1045 2518 697 6762 7454 6323 3595 4689 5660 4145 2107 5 1108 902 2610 980 3138 3785 2419 2114 2763 3561 1897 2405 6 851 1047 2536 698 2844 4069 2583 1651 2530 3484 1550 1674 G2.Bkg G3.Bkg G4.Bkg G5.Bkg G6.Bkg G7.Bkg 1 2561 1598 1506 1696 2667 1244 2 2527 1641 1196 1553 2569 848 3 2496 1902 1501 1644 2808 1154 4 2663 1607 1162 1577 2544 857 5 2528 1847 1445 1713 2767 1142 6 2648 1591 1114 1528 2668 870 ``` ::: ::: We'll pull the three pieces out of this table one at a time. ### rowData — feature information The first two columns describe each gene, so they become the `rowData`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} rdata <- deRisi[, 1:2] head(rdata) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ORF Name 1 YHR007C ERG11 2 YBR218C PYC2 3 YAL051W FUN43 4 YAL053W 5 YAL054C ACS1 6 YAL055W ``` ::: ::: ### colData — sample information The sample information isn't in the file, so we supply it ourselves. Each of the seven columns of measurements is a timepoint in the experiment: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cdata <- DataFrame(sample = paste("Sample", 0:6), timepoint = 0:6, hours = c(0, 9.5, 11.5, 13.5, 15.5, 18.5, 20.5)) cdata ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` DataFrame with 7 rows and 3 columns sample timepoint hours 1 Sample 0 0 0.0 2 Sample 1 1 9.5 3 Sample 2 2 11.5 4 Sample 3 3 13.5 5 Sample 4 4 15.5 6 Sample 5 5 18.5 7 Sample 6 6 20.5 ``` ::: ::: ### assays — the data The DeRisi experiment recorded four *different* measurements for every gene at every timepoint: | assay | description | |-------|-------------| | `R` | Red foreground fluorescence | | `G` | Green foreground fluorescence | | `Rb` | Red background fluorescence | | `Gb` | Green background fluorescence | Each becomes its own matrix, sliced out of the numeric columns: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} R <- as.matrix(deRisi[, 3:9]) G <- as.matrix(deRisi[, 10:16]) Rb <- as.matrix(deRisi[, 17:23]) Gb <- as.matrix(deRisi[, 24:30]) ``` ::: ### Aligning the names Here is the rule that makes the whole container trustworthy. The constructor **checks that the pieces line up**: the row names of every assay matrix must match the row names of `rowData`, and the column names of every assay matrix must match the row names of `colData`. If they don't, you get an error rather than a silent mismatch — the constructor refuses to build something inconsistent. So we set those names explicitly. Genes (rows) are keyed by their ORF identifier; samples (columns) by their sample name: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} rownames(rdata) <- rdata$ORF rownames(cdata) <- cdata$sample for (m in c("R", "G", "Rb", "Gb")) { mat <- get(m) rownames(mat) <- rdata$ORF colnames(mat) <- cdata$sample assign(m, mat) } ``` ::: ### Putting it together ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} se <- SummarizedExperiment(assays = list(R = R, G = G, Rb = Rb, Gb = Gb), rowData = rdata, colData = cdata) se ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` class: SummarizedExperiment dim: 6102 7 metadata(0): assays(4): R G Rb Gb rownames(6102): YHR007C YBR218C ... YPR203W YPR204W rowData names(2): ORF Name colnames(7): Sample 0 Sample 1 ... Sample 5 Sample 6 colData names(3): sample timepoint hours ``` ::: ::: One object now holds four aligned assays, the gene table, and the sample table. The constructor accepted it, which means everything lines up. ::: {.callout-warning} ## When the constructor complains If you ever see an error about non-matching dimensions or names when building a `SummarizedExperiment`, that is the container doing its job. Check that each matrix is genes × samples (not transposed), and that its `rownames`/`colnames` match `rowData`/`colData`. The error is annoying once; the silent mismatch it prevents is annoying for the life of the paper. ::: ## Adding a derived assay Real analysis rarely stops at the raw numbers. A natural quantity here is the background-corrected **log ratio** of red to green — a standard summary of two-color microarray signal. Because we compute it from assays that are already aligned, the result drops straight back into the object as a fifth assay, aligned forever: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} logRatios <- log2((assay(se, "R") - assay(se, "Rb")) / (assay(se, "G") - assay(se, "Gb"))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Warning: NaNs produced ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} assays(se)$logRatios <- logRatios assayNames(se) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "R" "G" "Rb" "Gb" "logRatios" ``` ::: ::: That is a real benefit worth pausing on: you can keep raw and processed measurements *in the same object*, each guaranteed to refer to the same genes and samples. Reach for any of them by name: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} head(assay(se, "logRatios")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Sample 0 Sample 1 Sample 2 Sample 3 Sample 4 Sample 5 YHR007C -1.2204686 NaN NaN 2.70275677 1.6545902 5.260867 YBR218C NaN NaN 2.9757832 2.39231742 1.9319816 3.983313 YAL051W 0.1135715 NaN NaN NaN -1.3681061 2.138654 YAL053W -1.3753298 NaN NaN 0.05044902 1.0906497 5.215440 YAL054C 0.2706476 0.333657387 0.0000000 0.31420165 0.3165815 NaN YAL055W 0.6209723 -0.001745548 0.2683547 0.11082813 0.4931189 NaN Sample 6 YHR007C 4.8223618 YBR218C NaN YAL051W 1.2205754 YAL053W 0.8875253 YAL054C NaN YAL055W NaN ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hist(assay(se, "logRatios"), breaks = 50, main = "DeRisi log ratios", xlab = "log2(R/G)") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Distribution of background-corrected log ratios across the DeRisi time course.](bioc-se-building_files/figure-html/fig-derisi-hist-1.png){#fig-derisi-hist width=672} ::: ::: ## A clustering heatmap of informative genes With 6,400 genes, no heatmap can show them all — nor would you want it to. As in the previous chapter, we keep the **variable** genes, because a gene whose log ratio barely moves across the time course carries no information about the diauxic shift; the genes that rise and fall are the informative ones. We rank by standard deviation and keep the top 50. The log-ratio calculation produces some non-finite values (a background-corrected signal can go negative, and `log2` of a negative number is `NaN`), so we first keep only genes measured cleanly at every timepoint: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} lr <- assay(se, "logRatios") lr <- lr[rowSums(!is.finite(lr)) == 0, ] # genes finite at all 7 timepoints top <- head(order(apply(lr, 1, sd), decreasing = TRUE), 50) lr_top <- lr[top, ] dim(lr_top) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 50 7 ``` ::: ::: Now the heatmap. Two deliberate choices: we **don't** cluster the columns (`cluster_cols = FALSE`) so the samples stay in time order and we can read each gene's trajectory left to right; and we **do** cluster the rows, which groups genes that move together. The column annotation — the time in hours — comes straight from `colData`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(pheatmap) ann <- as.data.frame(colData(se)[, "hours", drop = FALSE]) pheatmap(lr_top, cluster_cols = FALSE, # keep samples in time order cluster_rows = TRUE, # group co-regulated genes annotation_col = ann, show_rownames = FALSE, scale = "row", main = "Top 50 variable genes (DeRisi)") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The 50 most variable genes across the DeRisi diauxic-shift time course. Columns are held in time order; rows (genes) are clustered, grouping co-regulated genes. The annotation bar (hours) comes directly from colData.](bioc-se-building_files/figure-html/fig-derisi-heatmap-1.png){#fig-derisi-heatmap width=672} ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note} ## Unsupervised clustering, again — now on the genes Clustering the **rows** here groups genes purely by how similarly their expression moves over time, with no labels supplied — the same *unsupervised* idea you met in the [previous chapter](bioc-summarizedexperiment.qmd), now pointed at features instead of samples. Blocks of genes that rise together (or fall together) across the diauxic shift show up as bands. That is exactly the structure the [k-means chapter](kmeans.qmd) sets out to find formally on this very dataset; the heatmap is the quick, visual version of the same question. ::: ## Saving and sharing Here is the part that makes a collaborator's day. Your experiment — four raw assays, a derived one, the gene table, the sample table, and any notes — is a single R object. Save it to a single file: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # In practice you'd give it a real name, e.g. "derisi_experiment.rds". path <- tempfile(fileext = ".rds") saveRDS(se, path) ``` ::: Anyone who receives that file reads it back and has *everything*, already aligned, with nothing to re-link: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} se2 <- readRDS(path) se2 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` class: SummarizedExperiment dim: 6102 7 metadata(0): assays(5): R G Rb Gb logRatios rownames(6102): YHR007C YBR218C ... YPR203W YPR204W rowData names(2): ORF Name colnames(7): Sample 0 Sample 1 ... Sample 5 Sample 6 colData names(3): sample timepoint hours ``` ::: ::: No "which spreadsheet had the sample labels?", no "are the columns in the same order?". The object is self-describing. Stash provenance in `metadata()` and it rides along too: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} metadata(se)$processing <- "background-corrected log2 ratios; built in the RBioc Book" metadata(se)$date <- "2026-06-06" saveRDS(se, path) metadata(readRDS(path)) # the notes survive the round trip ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $processing [1] "background-corrected log2 ratios; built in the RBioc Book" $date [1] "2026-06-06" ``` ::: ::: This is also how published datasets are distributed: many arrive as ready-made `SummarizedExperiment` objects through Bioconductor's `ExperimentHub` and data packages (the `airway` package from the last chapter is exactly this). You load one line and get an analysis-ready object — because the author saved it in this shape. ## Why this is worth it: the ecosystem payoff Step back and ask what you actually *gained* by building this object instead of keeping a few matrices around. - **It can't silently desync.** Every subset, every new assay, stays aligned. - **It carries its own context.** Feature annotation, sample annotation, and experiment notes travel with the numbers, in one file. - **It is the common currency of Bioconductor.** This is the big one. Hundreds of analysis packages — `DESeq2` and `edgeR` and `limma` for differential expression, `scran` and `scater` for single cell, and many more — *take a `SummarizedExperiment` and hand one back*. You don't reshape your data for each tool; you build the object once and plug it into all of them. - **It is the root of a family.** The `SingleCellExperiment` you'll meet in the [single-cell chapter](single_cell/setup.qmd) and the `TreeSummarizedExperiment` in the [microbiome chapter](310_microbiome.qmd) are both `SummarizedExperiment`s with extra parts bolted on. Learn this shape once and those feel familiar immediately. The [GEOquery chapter](geoquery.qmd) and the [k-means chapter](kmeans.qmd) both hand you data in exactly this form. Build it once; everything downstream speaks the same language. ## Summary You took a flat spreadsheet and assembled it into a `SummarizedExperiment` — extracting `rowData`, supplying `colData`, building four assay matrices, and letting the constructor enforce that they all line up. You added a derived log-ratio assay that stays aligned, drew an unsupervised clustering heatmap of the most informative genes, and saved the whole thing to one self-describing file that carries its provenance. Most importantly, you now hold an object that the rest of the Bioconductor ecosystem accepts directly. ## Exercises ::: {.cell} ::: 1. **Build a tiny one.** Create a `SummarizedExperiment` from a 4 × 3 matrix of your choosing, a `rowData` with a `gene` column, and a `colData` with a `group` column. Confirm its `dim()`. 2. **Break it on purpose.** Try to build a `SummarizedExperiment` where the assay has 3 columns but `colData` has 4 rows. What happens, and why is that a good thing? 3. **Add a derived assay.** To the DeRisi `se`, add an assay called `Rcorr` equal to `R - Rb` (red minus red background). Confirm it appears in `assayNames(se)`. 4. **Save and reload.** Save the DeRisi `se` to a temporary file, read it back, and confirm the assay names and `metadata()` survived. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Solutions ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # 1. a minimal SummarizedExperiment m <- matrix(1:12, nrow = 4, dimnames = list(paste0("g", 1:4), paste0("s", 1:3))) rd <- DataFrame(gene = paste0("g", 1:4), row.names = paste0("g", 1:4)) cd <- DataFrame(group = c("a", "a", "b"), row.names = paste0("s", 1:3)) tiny <- SummarizedExperiment(assays = list(counts = m), rowData = rd, colData = cd) dim(tiny) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 4 3 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # 2. mismatched dimensions -> the constructor errors (a feature, not a bug): # it refuses to build an object whose pieces don't line up, so you can never # end up with sample labels pointing at the wrong columns. try(SummarizedExperiment(assays = list(x = m[, 1:3]), colData = DataFrame(group = letters[1:4]))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Error in `rownames<-`(`*tmp*`, value = .get_colnames_from_first_assay(assays)) : invalid rownames length ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # 3. a derived assay, aligned automatically assays(se)$Rcorr <- assay(se, "R") - assay(se, "Rb") assayNames(se) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "R" "G" "Rb" "Gb" "logRatios" "Rcorr" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # 4. round-trip through a file f <- tempfile(fileext = ".rds") saveRDS(se, f) back <- readRDS(f) assayNames(back) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "R" "G" "Rb" "Gb" "logRatios" "Rcorr" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} metadata(back) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $processing [1] "background-corrected log2 ratios; built in the RBioc Book" $date [1] "2026-06-06" ``` ::: ::: :::
